summary: This informational memo is a guide to finding useful information on the Internet, as a way to improve on how hard it was to locate resources then. The author describes techniques to make useful sources easier to reach, with the goal of hiding the route to them.

eli5.summary: The Internet is full of treasure, but finding it is tricky. This paper is like a treasure map, showing ways to find good information more easily.

questions: how to find information on the internet in 1993
subtitle: A 1993 field guide to where the useful files, catalogs, directories and services lived on the Internet, and how to reach them.

tldr.problem: The network held a huge amount of information, but people needed to know it existed, whether it mattered, and how to find it again.
tldr.mechanism: The memo is an annotated index of pointers: lists and bibliographies, library catalogs, anonymous FTP sites, information centers, campus information systems, bulletin boards, WHOIS directories, books and periodicals, each with instructions for reaching it.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo (FYI 10) that obsoletes RFC 1290. It is a snapshot of early 1993 practice, not a protocol, and its addresses and costs are specific to that moment.

facts.label: Dedicated T1 cost
facts.value: Up to $4,000 per month plus line charges

today: RFC 1402 is an Informational memo and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It is a historical snapshot of how people found resources in 1993; it obsoleted RFC 1290.

sections.title: The Problem of Finding Information
sections.content:
RFC 1402 is an Informational memo by Jerry Martin of Ohio State University, published in January 1993 as FYI 10. It does not specify a standard. It obsoletes RFC 1290.

The author lists three obstacles. First, you must know the information exists, so most of the documents listed are pointers to the final information. Second, you must know whether it is important or relevant, and librarians can help with that. Third, it must be indexed so researchers can find it. The memo calls that the hardest task, because network information is always moving, growing, changing and dying.

The stated goal is to make the route to these sources invisible to the user. The author admits that at the time this was not easy to do.
sections.eli5: There is a mountain of information, but nobody has labeled the shelves. The author wants to point you to the good stuff so you do not have to dig for it.

sections.title: Getting Access to the Internet
sections.content:
The memo explains how an ordinary person could get on the network. The most common way is electronic mail, which works through many gateways from other networks and services such as CompuServe. A direct connection adds abilities that e-mail lacks: Telnet to log in to a remote computer, and FTP to transfer files from one.

For people without an institutional connection, the memo describes buying access: an account on a public access bulletin board system, a dial-in account with a service provider, or a dedicated connection. It quotes monthly costs from $250 for a dialup 9600-bps connection to $4,000 for a T1 line, plus line charges, and lists providers such as ALTERNET, PSINet, CERFnet, ANSNET, MSEN and OARnet with the speeds they offered.

These prices and providers come from a Usenet FAQ excerpt that the memo reproduces. They describe 1993 only.
sections.eli5: To get into the library you need a door. A school computer is the easiest door. Otherwise you pay a company a monthly fee to let you in.

sections.title: Lists, Indexes and Library Catalogs
sections.content:
Section 2 is a catalog of documents and programs that index other resources. Each entry gives a short description and a Source, usually the anonymous FTP host, directory and file to fetch. Examples include the Internet Resource Guide, a list of all anonymous FTP sites, an index of RFCs that includes the user guides RFC 1118 and RFC 1392, the Interest Groups list of mailing lists, and regional network policies.

The same section covers programs such as Hytelnet, and the World Wide Web, which the memo describes as merging information retrieval and hypertext into a global information system. The memo says you can try a simple line mode browser by Telnetting to info.cern.ch. Section 3 points to library catalogs and databases reachable over the network.
sections.eli5: This part is a list of lists, like a table of contents for the whole library. Each entry tells you which door to knock on.

sections.title: Anonymous FTP and Archie
sections.content:
Section 4 is about anonymous FTP sites, which let anyone fetch files without an account of their own. The memo names popular archives such as Washington University (wuarchive.wustl.edu), the Kermit archive at Columbia, and NCSA software for network access from PCs.

To find a particular program, the memo recommends archie (Archive Server Listing Service). Archie goes to every site that offers anonymous FTP files, collects the file structure from that site, and places it in a database that can be searched. The author gives a worked example: looking up a shareware program named in a magazine, logging in as archie on archie.ans.net, and getting back the host and directory where it is stored.
sections.eli5: Anonymous FTP is a free lending shelf where you do not need a library card. Archie is the helper who remembers which shelf holds the book you want.

sections.title: People, Centers and Directories
sections.content:
Section 5 lists Network Information Centers (NICs), the places to ask for help: the main Internet NIC run by Government Systems, Inc., the NSF Network Service Center, NSFNET Information Services, SRI's Network Information Systems Center, BITNET and NASA's NSI. Section 6 points to monthly NSF network statistics files.

Section 7 covers Campuswide Information Systems (CWISes), where a menu hides the network details so users only need to know what they want. The memo notes many CWISes were converting to Gopher. Section 8 lists bulletin boards and Freenets reachable by Telnet, such as the Cleveland Freenet. Section 9 covers WHOIS, a lookup for a person's e-mail address, and adds that there is no master list of e-mail addresses on the network, so the easiest first step may be to phone and ask. Sections 10 and 11 list books and free periodicals, and section 12 is a glossary.
sections.eli5: If you get lost, there are help desks, campus information kiosks and phone books. This part tells you where each one is.

references.text: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Internet, RFC 1118.
